You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Indian Economy for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course. Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the
book's own terms and spellings.
Course: "3. Money" · subject: Indian Economy · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.

Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.

[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-24.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.

items.content: An Indian currency note is not a promissory note in the legal sense, even though it contains a promise clause.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a currency note compare with a legal promissory note?
teacher_understanding.answer: A promise clause appears on the currency note, but the page says this does not make it a promissory note in law.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the decisive legal distinction?
teacher_understanding.answer: The quoted Section 4 definition expressly excludes bank-notes and currency-notes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the presence of a promise insufficient?
teacher_understanding.answer: Legal categories depend on the statutory definition, not simply on similar wording on two documents.

items.exam_note: Trap: a promise clause does not establish legal classification as a promissory note.

terms.plain_meaning: नोट पर भुगतान का वादा लिखने वाला हिस्सा
terms.everyday_image: किसी कागज़ पर पैसे लौटाने का वादा लिखा होना

why_chain.step: Similar wording can make two documents look legally identical.
Section 4 excludes currency-notes, so wording alone cannot decide their category.

unpack.example_or_place: The promise printed on an Indian currency note.
unpack.consequence: Read the statutory exclusion before classifying the instrument.
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish everyday meaning from legal meaning.

items.content: Section 4 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881: A promissory note is: ”An instrument in writing (not being a bank-note or a currency-note) containing an unconditional undertaking.
items.type_note: The year identifies the statute; the content defines a legal instrument rather than narrating events.

teacher_understanding.question: What elements of the definition are quoted?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a written instrument containing an unconditional undertaking, with bank-notes and currency-notes expressly excluded.

teacher_understanding.question: Which provision supports the exclusion?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page cites Section 4 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, especially the words 'not being a bank-note or a currency-note'.

teacher_understanding.question: How should unconditional undertaking be understood?
teacher_understanding.answer: It means a definite commitment not dependent on an uncertain condition, unlike 'I will pay if my business succeeds'.

items.exam_note: Remember Section 4 and the express exclusion; this is only the extract printed here.

terms.plain_meaning: ऐसा पक्का वादा जिसके साथ कोई 'अगर' नहीं लगा है
terms.everyday_image: 'पैसे दूँगा' और 'नौकरी मिली तो पैसे दूँगा' में फर्क

why_chain.step: A payment commitment needs a clear legal meaning.
The quoted definition specifies writing and an unconditional undertaking while excluding currency-notes.

unpack.example_or_place: Compare an unconditional written payment promise with a currency note.
unpack.consequence: The statutory exception resolves the apparent contradiction in i1.
unpack.level_extra: Do not present this incomplete quotation as the whole statutory definition.

items.content: MANI App
MANI (Mobile Aided Note Identifier): It is a free mobile app launched by the Reserve Bank of India on 1 January 2020.

teacher_understanding.question: When and by whom was MANI launched?
teacher_understanding.answer: The Reserve Bank of India launched the free Mobile Aided Note Identifier app on 1 January 2020.

teacher_understanding.question: Why was the app introduced?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its stated purpose is to help visually impaired persons independently identify Indian banknote denominations.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a free mobile tool support this purpose?
teacher_understanding.answer: It can reduce dependence on another person for reading a note’s value without charging an app purchase price.

items.exam_note: Know expansion, RBI, free access and launch date.

terms.plain_meaning: फोन की मदद से नोट की कीमत पहचानने वाला app
terms.everyday_image: फोन नोट देखकर उसकी रकम बताता है

why_chain.step: Reading a printed denomination can be difficult for someone with impaired vision.
RBI launched a free identification app for independent use.

unpack.example_or_place: Identifying money received as change.
unpack.consequence: Links RBI’s currency role with accessibility.
unpack.level_extra: Do not confuse the developer institution with a commercial bank.

items.content: To help visually impaired persons identify the denomination of Indian banknotes independently.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is independent denomination identification important?
teacher_understanding.answer: Reading printed values may be difficult for visually impaired users; independent identification reduces the need to ask another person.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page show MANI helping these users?
teacher_understanding.answer: The graphic shows scanning either side of a banknote and providing denomination information through audio, with vibration for users with vision and hearing impairment.

items.exam_note: Purpose is denomination identification; the page does not establish counterfeit authentication.

terms.plain_meaning: नोट पर लिखी रकम, जैसे ₹100 या ₹500
terms.everyday_image: दुकान पर ₹100 और ₹500 का नोट अलग करना

why_chain.step: A user needs to know the value of money being received or paid.
MANI helps visually impaired persons identify that value independently.

unpack.example_or_place: Checking a banknote before paying a shopkeeper.
unpack.consequence: Accessibility supports independent transactions.
unpack.level_extra: Keep denomination recognition distinct from genuineness testing.

items.content: Android and iOS both.

teacher_understanding.question: Which mobile platforms does MANI support?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page lists both Android and iOS rather than restricting access to one platform.

teacher_understanding.question: What wording supports cross-platform availability?
teacher_understanding.answer: The explicit bullet says 'Android and iOS both.'

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this matter for accessibility?
teacher_understanding.answer: People using either major phone platform can use the tool without changing platforms for this purpose.

items.exam_note: Reject a statement limiting MANI to Android alone.

terms.everyday_image: Android फोन और iPhone

why_chain.step: Users own different types of smartphones.
Support for both platforms broadens access.

unpack.example_or_place: Android phones and iPhones.
unpack.consequence: Platform choice is not restricted to one of these two systems.
unpack.level_extra: A simple statement-combination fact.

items.content: Works offline after installation
items.type_note: This is an operating capability, not a sequence of process stages.

teacher_understanding.question: What connectivity feature is stated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Once installed, MANI can work offline.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this feature confirmed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both the bullet and the graphic explicitly say it works offline after installation.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is offline operation useful?
teacher_understanding.answer: Denomination identification need not depend on an active internet connection at the time of use.

items.exam_note: Distinguish installation from subsequent use.

terms.plain_meaning: उस समय internet जुड़े बिना काम करना
terms.everyday_image: फोन में पहले से रखी फोटो बिना data के खोलना

why_chain.step: A user may need to identify cash where connectivity is poor.
Offline operation after installation removes that immediate connectivity dependence.

unpack.example_or_place: A shop with weak mobile data coverage.
unpack.consequence: Do not interpret offline operation as requiring no initial installation.
unpack.level_extra: The qualifying words 'after installation' matter.

items.content: Supports 15 Languages, including Hindi and English

teacher_understanding.question: What language support is stated?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page reports 15 languages and names Hindi and English among them.

teacher_understanding.answer: No; only Hindi and English are named, so the remaining languages cannot be enumerated from this page.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does multilingual support matter?
teacher_understanding.answer: An audio-based accessibility tool is more usable when the user understands the language of its output.

items.exam_note: Retain the page’s count without inventing the remaining language names.

terms.plain_meaning: app में 15 भाषाओं का सहारा मिलता है
terms.everyday_image: फोन में अपनी समझ की भाषा चुनना

why_chain.step: Users may not understand the same language.
Multiple language options make the tool usable for more people.

unpack.example_or_place: Hindi or English language use.
unpack.consequence: Accessibility includes language as well as sensory access.
unpack.level_extra: Treat this as the book’s stated feature count.

Either side supplies an accepted scan according to the graphic.

teacher_understanding.question: Why use sound rather than only on-screen text?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sound allows a user who cannot easily read the screen to receive the note’s value.

terms.everyday_image: फोन रकम बोलकर सुनाए

unpack.example_or_place: Hearing a note’s value from a phone.
unpack.consequence: The user need not rely solely on sight.
unpack.level_extra: Input is visual scanning; output can be audible.

teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies vibration for users with both vision and hearing impairment.

teacher_understanding.answer: The panel explicitly mentions users with vision and hearing impairment.

teacher_understanding.question: Why add vibration when audio already exists?
teacher_understanding.answer: Audio may not be accessible to a person with hearing impairment; vibration provides a touch-based signal.

items.exam_note: Image-only accessibility detail; do not omit dual sensory impairment.

terms.everyday_image: silent mode में फोन का हाथ में हिलना

why_chain.step: Some users cannot readily use sight or hearing for feedback.
Vibration offers a touch-based route for feedback.

unpack.example_or_place: A vibrating phone held in the hand.
unpack.consequence: Accessibility is not limited to spoken output.

teacher_understanding.answer: MANI works without an active internet connection after installation.

teacher_understanding.answer: The app must already have been installed.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is this useful in daily transactions?
teacher_understanding.answer: A user may need to identify cash even where mobile connectivity is unavailable.

unpack.consequence: Connectivity loss need not prevent use.

items.content: Demonetization
Demonetization means the REMOVAL of legal tender status of currency notes. It becomes invalid for transactions.

teacher_understanding.question: What changes in demonetisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: The note loses its legal-tender status; the page describes it as becoming invalid for transactions.

teacher_understanding.question: Which words define the decisive test?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page emphasises 'REMOVAL of legal tender status', not merely stopping printing or withdrawing notes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is legal-tender status more important than physical possession?
teacher_understanding.answer: A person can still hold the paper note after its legal payment status changes; the policy changes its legal role, not its physical existence.

items.exam_note: Core definition distinguishes demonetisation from withdrawal.

terms.plain_meaning: पैसे के रूप में भुगतान के लिए कानून से मिली मान्यता
terms.everyday_image: हाथ में रखा नोट और उसे भुगतान में मान्यता मिलना दो अलग बातें

why_chain.step: A currency policy can change a note’s legal payment status.
Removal of that status is what the page calls demonetisation.

unpack.example_or_place: Existing ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes in the 2016 announcement.
unpack.consequence: Use legal status, not disappearance from circulation, as the test.
unpack.level_extra: Avoid assuming that every withdrawn note is demonetised.

items.content: India has carried out three major demonetisations—in 1946, 1978, and 2016.

teacher_understanding.question: Which three years does the book identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lists 1946, 1978 and 2016 as India’s three major demonetisations.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is 2023 not a fourth event in this list?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page says the ₹2,000 notes withdrawn in 2023 remained legal tender.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the chronology be retained without confusing events?
teacher_understanding.answer: Attach each year to its government and affected denominations using the adjacent table, rather than memorising four years as equivalent events.

items.exam_note: Chronology and the exclusion of 2023 are statement-combination targets.

why_chain.step: Different currency events can be confused when only years are memorised.
Classify by legal-tender removal, keeping 2023 outside the three major demonetisations.

unpack.consequence: The table adds the denomination and government associations.
unpack.level_extra: Keep pre-independence 1946 distinct from the later two events.

items.content: 8 November 2016: PM Modi announced that existing: ₹500 notes and ₹1,000 notes would cease to be legal tender from midnight.

teacher_understanding.question: When was the announcement made and when did the stated change take effect?
teacher_understanding.answer: PM Modi announced it on 8 November 2016, with the existing ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes ceasing to be legal tender from midnight.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this event qualify as demonetisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: The existing notes lost legal-tender status, which is the page’s defining criterion.

teacher_understanding.question: Which wording prevents overgeneralisation to every ₹500 note?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page specifies 'existing' notes in that announcement.

items.exam_note: Distinguish announcement date, midnight effect and affected existing notes.

terms.plain_meaning: भुगतान के पैसे के रूप में कानूनी मान्यता खत्म होना
terms.everyday_image: रात के समय एक नोट की कानूनी स्थिति बदलने की समयरेखा

why_chain.step: A legal currency change needs an effective time and specified notes.
The announcement names existing ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes and midnight.

unpack.example_or_place: 8 November 2016 announcement.
unpack.consequence: Introduces the need for replacement currency discussed below.
unpack.level_extra: Do not add unstated policy objectives to this page’s account.

items.content: A withdrawal of ₹2,000 notes in 2023, which was not a demonetisation because the notes remained legal tender.
items.type_note: The combined sentence explains classification through retained legal-tender status; the year is contextual.

teacher_understanding.question: Why was the 2023 ₹2,000 withdrawal not demonetisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: The notes retained legal-tender status, so the defining removal of that status did not occur.

teacher_understanding.question: How should withdrawal and demonetisation be distinguished?
teacher_understanding.answer: Withdrawal concerns taking notes out of circulation; demonetisation concerns removing their legal-tender status. These need not coincide.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page contrast 2016 and 2023?
teacher_understanding.answer: The affected existing notes in 2016 ceased to be legal tender, whereas the withdrawn ₹2,000 notes in 2023 remained legal tender.

items.exam_note: Central trap: withdrawal does not necessarily mean demonetisation.

terms.plain_meaning: नोट को चलन से वापस लेने की कार्रवाई
terms.everyday_image: नोट बैंक में लौट रहा है, लेकिन उसकी legal tender मान्यता अलग सवाल है

why_chain.step: A note can be taken out of circulation without cancelling its legal status.
The page says ₹2,000 notes retained legal-tender status in the 2023 withdrawal.

unpack.example_or_place: 2023 withdrawal of ₹2,000 notes.
unpack.consequence: 2023 must not be counted with the three demonetisations.
unpack.level_extra: Test two separate propositions: circulation action and legal status.

items.content: 2016-Nov: RBI introduced ₹2000 note, to meet the currency requirement of the economy in an [a] faster manner after demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1000

teacher_understanding.question: When did RBI introduce the ₹2,000 note?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page places its introduction in November 2016, following demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why was the note introduced according to this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: It was introduced to meet the economy’s currency requirement more quickly.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a larger denomination help supply a given value of cash?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fewer individual notes are needed: ₹2,000 of value requires one ₹2,000 note but four ₹500 notes.

items.exam_note: Link introduction date to the stated replacement-currency need.

terms.plain_meaning: लेन-देन के लिए अर्थव्यवस्था को जितनी नकदी चाहिए
terms.everyday_image: दुकान, ग्राहक और मजदूरी देने के लिए नकदी चाहिए

why_chain.step: After demonetisation, the economy needed replacement currency.
A higher denomination supplies a given cash value through fewer pieces of paper.

unpack.example_or_place: One ₹2,000 note compared with four ₹500 notes.
unpack.consequence: Introduces the first stage of the ₹2,000 note’s later printing and withdrawal timeline.
unpack.level_extra: The arithmetic explains the stated rationale; it is not an additional quoted policy claim.

items.content: 2018–19: printing of ₹2000 banknotes was stopped.

teacher_understanding.question: When does the page say printing stopped?
teacher_understanding.answer: It gives 2018–19 for stopping the printing of ₹2,000 banknotes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should stopping printing not be read as demonetisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: Stopping new production does not itself remove legal-tender status from notes already issued.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this event fit the chronology?
teacher_understanding.answer: It follows the November 2016 introduction and precedes the 2023 withdrawal described on the page.

items.exam_note: Do not equate cessation of printing with withdrawal or demonetisation.

terms.plain_meaning: नए नोट बनाना
terms.everyday_image: नई प्रतियाँ छापना बंद हो, फिर भी पुरानी प्रतियाँ मौजूद रहती हैं

why_chain.step: Students can confuse making new notes with the status of existing notes.
A printing stop concerns fresh supply, not automatic cancellation of existing notes.

unpack.example_or_place: ₹2,000 note printing in 2018–19.
unpack.consequence: Keep production, circulation and legal status as separate dimensions.
unpack.level_extra: The page does not give a reason for stopping printing.

items.content: 2023-May-23rd: RBI ordered people to get it exchanged with other notes.

teacher_understanding.question: What date does the page print for the exchange instruction?
teacher_understanding.answer: It prints '2023-May-23rd' and attributes the exchange instruction to RBI.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is this exchange instruction not evidence of demonetisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page explicitly says the withdrawn ₹2,000 notes remained legal tender.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the exact printed date be treated in teaching?
teacher_understanding.answer: Treat it cautiously as the page’s date; distinguish an announcement date from the start of an exchange facility before using it as a precise date fact.

items.exam_note: Exact date needs verification; preserve the printed statement without silently correcting it.

terms.plain_meaning: एक नोट के बदले उतनी ही रकम के दूसरे नोट लेना
terms.everyday_image: ₹2,000 देकर बराबर रकम के छोटे नोट लेना

why_chain.step: Withdrawal requires a way to replace the affected note with other notes.
The page describes RBI directing exchange while retaining legal-tender status.

unpack.example_or_place: Exchange of ₹2,000 notes for other denominations.
unpack.consequence: Exchange is an operational action, not the defining legal test.
unpack.level_extra: Flag the date distinction rather than memorising an unverified announcement date.

items.content: Gresham’s Law
It states that "bad money drives out good money" when both are accepted as legal tender at the same face value.

teacher_understanding.question: What does Gresham’s Law state here?
teacher_understanding.answer: When both monies are legal tender at the same face value, bad money drives good money out of circulation.

teacher_understanding.question: What condition qualifies the slogan on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both must be accepted as legal tender at the same face value; the following bullets add fixed exchange value and intrinsic undervaluation.

teacher_understanding.question: Why would people spend bad money and keep good money?
teacher_understanding.answer: If both settle the same payment but one contains more valuable material, people have an incentive to spend the less intrinsically valuable money and retain, melt or otherwise remove the more valuable money from ordinary circulation.

teacher_understanding.question: How should bad and good be interpreted?
teacher_understanding.answer: They refer to relative intrinsic value under the legal valuation, not necessarily counterfeit versus genuine or physically dirty versus clean notes.

items.exam_note: The conditional mechanism matters more than the slogan; good money leaves circulation, not existence.

items.content: Demonetization
Demonetization means the REMOVAL of legal tender status of currency notes. It becomes invalid for transactions.

teacher_understanding.question: What changes in demonetisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: The note loses its legal-tender status; the page describes it as becoming invalid for transactions.

teacher_understanding.question: Which words define the decisive test?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page emphasises 'REMOVAL of legal tender status', not merely stopping printing or withdrawing notes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is legal-tender status more important than physical possession?
teacher_understanding.answer: A person can still hold the paper note after its legal payment status changes; the policy changes its legal role, not its physical existence.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this event qualify as demonetisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: The existing notes lost legal-tender status, which is the page’s defining criterion.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the correct distinction between the announcement and exchange dates?

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the page distinguish this withdrawal from demonetisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: The accompanying text explicitly says the ₹2,000 notes remained legal tender; their legal-tender status was not removed.

items.exam_note: Printed wording is misleading: withdrawal announced 19 May 2023; branch exchange began 23 May. Deposit and exchange were options; legal-tender status continued.

items.content: Gresham’s Law
It states that "bad money drives out good money" when both are accepted as legal tender at the same face value.

teacher_understanding.question: What does Gresham’s Law state here?
teacher_understanding.answer: When both monies are legal tender at the same face value, bad money drives good money out of circulation.

teacher_understanding.question: What condition qualifies the slogan on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both must be accepted as legal tender at the same face value; the following bullets add fixed exchange value and intrinsic undervaluation.

teacher_understanding.question: Why would people spend bad money and keep good money?
teacher_understanding.answer: If both settle the same payment but one contains more valuable material, people have an incentive to spend the less intrinsically valuable money and retain, melt or otherwise remove the more valuable money from ordinary circulation.

teacher_understanding.question: How should bad and good be interpreted?
teacher_understanding.answer: They refer to relative intrinsic value under the legal valuation, not necessarily counterfeit versus genuine or physically dirty versus clean notes.

items.exam_note: The conditional mechanism matters more than the slogan; good money leaves circulation, not existence.

why_chain.step: A payer can settle the same amount with two legally equal monies of different intrinsic worth.
Spending the less valuable one and saving the more valuable one reduces good money in circulation.

unpack.consequence: Explains why the law requires specific valuation conditions.
unpack.level_extra: Bad money is not shorthand for counterfeit currency.

items.content: Both currencies are legal tender.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the law require both monies to be legal tender?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its spending incentive depends on the less intrinsically valuable money still being legally usable to discharge the same payment.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page state this condition?
teacher_understanding.answer: It explicitly requires both currencies to be legal tender and describes both as accepted at the same face value.

items.exam_note: Do not apply the stated law indiscriminately to any two kinds of money.

why_chain.step: The payer needs a legally usable payment option.
If both qualify, the cheaper intrinsic option can be spent instead.

unpack.example_or_place: Two hypothetical legally accepted coin types.
unpack.consequence: Legal usability creates the basis for substitution in payments.
unpack.level_extra: This condition is about legal status, not physical appearance.

items.content: The government fixes their exchange value.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does fixed exchange value matter?
teacher_understanding.answer: A fixed legal valuation can prevent the more intrinsically valuable money from receiving a correspondingly higher payment value, creating an incentive to retain it.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the government enter the page’s statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page makes government-fixed exchange value a required condition of the law.

teacher_understanding.question: What if exchange values can adjust to intrinsic worth?
teacher_understanding.answer: The stated mechanism may not operate in the same way because the more valuable money can command a higher exchange value instead of being legally undervalued.

items.exam_note: Fixed legal valuation is a key qualification of the slogan.

terms.plain_meaning: एक पैसे के बदले दूसरे पैसे की तय रकम
terms.everyday_image: दो तरह के सिक्कों के बीच सरकार की तय बराबरी

why_chain.step: Different material worth would otherwise allow different exchange prices.
A fixed legal value can preserve a mismatch that rewards retaining the better money.

unpack.example_or_place: Hypothetical legally equal coins containing different quantities of valuable metal.
unpack.consequence: Connects the legal rule to intrinsic undervaluation in the next condition.
unpack.level_extra: Contrast fixed valuation with an adjustable market exchange value.

items.content: One currency is undervalued relative to its intrinsic value.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does intrinsic undervaluation drive good money out?
teacher_understanding.answer: If money’s material worth exceeds what its legal valuation recognises relative to the other money, spending it sacrifices value that can be preserved by retaining it.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this condition complete the mechanism?
teacher_understanding.answer: Legal equivalence creates a choice, and the intrinsic-value mismatch makes spending the less valuable money more attractive.

teacher_understanding.question: What mismatch does the page require?
teacher_understanding.answer: One currency must be undervalued relative to its intrinsic value.

teacher_understanding.question: What does drives out mean for the good money?
teacher_understanding.answer: It tends to be withheld from ordinary circulation, not necessarily destroyed or made illegal.

items.exam_note: Undervalued good money is retained; relatively overvalued bad money circulates.
